title: Dissolved Into Its Own Shareholders: The 1911 Decree, Six Months to Comply, and the Flag the Trust Asked For in 1914
participants: Standard Oil Company of New Jersey
U.S. Supreme Court (Chief Justice Edward D. White)
Circuit Court for the Eastern District of Missouri
William H. Libby (for Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The New Jersey holding company sits on the stocks of its subsidiaries and takes the return of the combination they make up. The Government sues under the Sherman Act of 1890 and the Circuit Court for the Eastern District of Missouri decrees that the combination be dissolved.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The remedy is not a sale to strangers. The fifth paragraph of the decree permits the distribution of the subsidiary stocks "among the shareholders of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey": the thing dissolved is handed, piece by piece, to the people who already owned it whole. The appellants' own complaint on appeal is not that the distribution was ordered but that the court presumed to limit how they carried it out.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The law itself is moved while the case is pending. Argued in March 1910, restored to the docket, reargued in January 1911 and decided on 15 May 1911, the case produces a Sherman Act read "in the light of reason", under which only unreasonable or undue restraints offend the statute. Justice Harlan, concurring in the affirmance, dissents from that reading in terms the record keeps: the Court, he writes, has "read into the act of Congress words which are not to be found there", and he warns that "illegitimate and unconstitutional practices get their first footing by silent approaches and slight deviations from legal modes of legal procedure".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The timetable is then relaxed at the trust's own request. The Court finds "the delay of thirty days allowed for executing the decree was too short and should be extended so as to embrace a period of at least six months", and strikes the injunction that would have stopped the New Jersey corporation and every subsidiary from carrying on interstate commerce until the stocks were transferred. Half a year to rearrange the succession, and not a day off the market while it happens.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: What remains of the prohibition is a rule against doing again what the decree had just done for them: paragraph 6 is construed as restraining the stockholders from "by any device whatever, recreating directly or indirectly the illegal combination which the decree dissolved", while expressly leaving them the power "to make normal and lawful contracts or agreements". Three years later the company writes to the Secretary of State asking the United States to obtain from the belligerent powers an exemption from seizure and inquiry for tankers moved to the American flag, citing the protection already given the six American steamers of the International Mercantile Marine Company — the flag applied for as an asset, and the precedent drawn from the shipping trust this atlas files at CC-1912-IMM.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Sherman Act of 1890, and the court-supervised reorganization practice of the 1890s railroads in which a judge's decree returns the property to its own owners in a new form — the receivership template, applied here to an antitrust remedy rather than an insolvency.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The rule of reason, and with it the dissolution that distributes instead of divesting: a remedy measured against a shareholder list, with a compliance window long enough to arrange the succession and no interruption of trade while it is arranged.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The subsidiary stocks pass to the holding company's own shareholders; the six-month extension and the struck injunction keep the business whole and trading throughout; and the surviving interest turns to the State Department for a flag the moment war threatens its fleet, citing a shipping trust's protection as the precedent.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That 1911 broke Standard Oil — that the Supreme Court ended the Rockefeller monopoly at the courthouse door, and the thirty-four successor companies went out to compete with one another.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The decree's own fifth paragraph permitted the subsidiary stocks to be distributed among the shareholders of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey, so the ownership the decree dissolved was the ownership it handed the pieces to; and the Supreme Court then lengthened the time for doing it from thirty days to at least six months and struck the injunction that would have halted the subsidiaries' interstate commerce in the meantime. What the decree forbade afterwards was recreating the combination "by any device whatever" — while expressly preserving the stockholders' power to make normal and lawful contracts.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States, 221 U.S. 1 (1911), decided 15 May 1911: the Sherman Act read "in the light of reason"; the combination held an unreasonable restraint; the thirty-day compliance window extended to at least six months; the paragraph 7 trade injunction held wrongly awarded; paragraph 6 construed to bar recreating the combination while preserving normal contracting; and Harlan, concurring in the affirmance, dissenting from the rule of reason. Three years on, William H. Libby for the company asks the Secretary of State to obtain a belligerent-power exemption from seizure for its re-flagged tankers, on the precedent of the International Mercantile Marine Company's six American steamers.

citations.title: Standard Oil Company of New Jersey v. United States, 221 U.S. 1 (1911)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read on CourtListener (the full report, headmatter through Harlan's separate opinion). Appeal from the Circuit Court for the Eastern District of Missouri; argued 14, 15, 16 March 1910; restored to the docket for reargument 11 April 1910; reargued 12, 13, 16, 17 January 1911; decided 15 May 1911. The syllabus states that the Anti-trust Act of 2 July 1890 "should be construed in the light of reason; and, as so construed, it prohibits all contracts and combination which amount to an unreasonable or undue restraint of trade in interstate commerce", and that the defendants' combination "is an unreasonable and undue restraint of trade in petroleum and its products". On the remedy the Court says: "We think that in view of the magnitude of the interests involved and their complexity that the delay of thirty days allowed for executing the decree was too short and should be extended so as to embrace a period of at least six months", and that the injunction provided for in paragraph 7 — against the New Jersey corporation and all the subsidiary companies carrying on interstate commerce until the dissolution was effected by transfer of the stocks — "should not have been awarded". It construes paragraph 6 "not as depriving the stockholders or corporations, after the dissolution of the combination, of the power to make normal and lawful contracts or agreements, but as restraining them from, by any device whatever, recreating directly or indirectly the illegal combination which the decree dissolved", and concludes "that the decree below was right and should be affirmed, except as to the minor matters concerning which we have indicated the decree should be modified." The appellants' assignment of errors records that "the court in s 5 permitted the distribution among the shareholders of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey of the stocks held by that company" and complains that it then limited the method of distribution. Justice Harlan, "while concurring in the general affirmance of the decree of the Circuit Court", dissents "from that part of the judgment of this court which directs the modification of the decree" and from the reading by which the Court "has now read into the act of Congress words which are not to be found there". The report does not state who held the successor stocks after distribution, and no post-decree ownership figure is taken from it.

citations.title: William H. Libby (for the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey) to the Secretary of State, New York, 18 August 1914, File No. 195.1/12 — Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States, 1914, Supplement, The World War, Document 767
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on the Office of the Historian site. A letter written "In behalf of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey" about American-owned vessels under foreign flags, "for the registration of which as American vessels provision has just been made" — the Ship Registry Act of 18 August 1914. Libby states the understanding that vessels transferred to the American flag "would receive the same protection from the Government of the United States as has been accorded to vessels heretofore flying the American flag (for instance, the six American steamers of the International Mercantile Marine Company)", warns that if the good faith of a transfer were inquired into "in the prize courts of belligerent powers" the inquiry "would involve the seizure and detention of the vessel, the costs and delay of a judicial examination, perhaps in a distant place, and the loss of time and freight", and asks: "it has occurred to us that our Government might, without prejudicing in any way any other class of cases, secure the assent of the powers engaged in the present conflict to the exemption from seizure and inquiry of vessels transferred to the American flag which were actually owned in this country before the war began." The letter argues from the Declaration of London, which it notes "has not, we believe, acquired the force of a treaty". This document is a company request for diplomatic protection of its shipping; it records no reply, no instruction to any belligerent, and no use of force, and nothing is claimed here beyond the request itself.
